method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: The dollar is near a three-week low: US shares slid on Thursday and investors bought US government bonds, pulling their yields down sharply. Layoffs are the fewest since July, though, and with oil high the Fed is still expected to hold on October 28 and raise rates in December.

EUR.text: France now pays the most over Germany to borrow since the 2011 debt crisis, with its budget stuck in parliament and a Moody's rating review on October 23. Euro-area households grew gloomier than expected, and economists at ING think France's troubles give the ECB less reason to hike, so the euro is sliding against the pound and the franc.

GBP.text: Above-forecast UK inflation, and rate-setters such as Megan Greene saying the energy shock could spread, have traders expecting at least three Bank of England hikes by April, starting November 5. That, plus money leaving the euro area, keeps the pound near $1.34; the October 28 budget is the main risk.

JPY.text: The yen had its best day in about a month, reaching about 157 per dollar, as falling share markets and Gulf attacks sent money to shelter and US bond yields eased. Bank of Japan officials keep a December hike in view; national inflation data is due October 23 and the bank meets October 29–30.

CHF.text: The franc hit a three-month high against the euro on Thursday as Gulf attacks, a slide in shares and France's debt worries sent money to shelter. Notes from the Swiss National Bank's September meeting say it no longer needs to stand extra ready to stop the franc rising.

CAD.text: The loonie has risen six days running to a one-month high, near 1.40 per US dollar, helped by Brent oil above $110 and bets on a Bank of Canada rate hike on October 28. Some strategists think markets expect too many hikes, since core inflation is below the bank's 2% target.

AUD.text: The Aussie reached a one-month high above 70 US cents after Reserve Bank of Australia officials warned inflation may run hotter. But Asian shares fell to a three-month low on Thursday, which tends to weigh on it; Australia's inflation figures on October 28 decide a November 3 hike.

NZD.text: New Zealand's inflation slowed to 3.7% in the third quarter, a little below forecasts and the central bank's own 3.9% projection. A rate hike on October 28 still looks likely, but the softer figure trims that bet and pulled the kiwi back just under 57 US cents.

XAU.text: Gold eased to about $4,070, near its low for the month, because markets see a US rate hike in December as very likely. Falling shares and Gulf attacks bring some shelter demand, but not enough to offset that.

OIL.text: Brent oil is at a five-month high above $111 after Iran claimed hits on seven Gulf ships, Houthi attacks reached Saudi Arabia's oil region, and reports said the US and Israel plan new strikes on Iran after the November 3 US election. With the Strait of Hormuz still largely shut, supply risk is growing even as the US releases fuel reserves and President Trump promises calm before the vote.

items.headline: Euro zone consumer confidence falls to -17.9 in October
items.story_title: Euro area: how households and firms are holding up
items.summary: Euro-area households grew gloomier in October than economists expected, as high energy costs bite.

beats.was: The European Commission's monthly consumer confidence survey asks households how they feel about money and the economy. It was already weak at -16.8 in September, with oil above $100 lifting fuel and heating bills.
beats.happened: The early October reading fell to -17.9, below the -17.0 economists expected. For the whole European Union it slipped to -17.3.
beats.means: Shoppers are getting more cautious, which points to softer spending and makes it harder for the European Central Bank to keep raising rates without hurting growth.
beats.fx: Weaker household mood + high energy bills → less room for ECB hikes than for Bank of England hikes, a mild drag on the euro.

impact.why: A bigger-than-expected drop in confidence points to weaker spending.

items.watch: The euro-area business surveys (flash PMIs) on October 23 for whether firms are slowing too.

items.headline: US jobless claims fell to 194,000 last week, lowest since July
items.story_title: US jobs: hiring slow, layoffs low
items.summary: Fewer Americans filed new claims for unemployment benefits last week than at any time since July, a sign layoffs remain rare.

beats.was: Weekly jobless claims count people newly applying for unemployment benefits, a quick read on layoffs. US hiring has been slow and the jobless rate rose to 4.2% last month, but companies have mostly kept their staff.
beats.happened: New claims fell to 194,000 from 200,000 the week before, the lowest in three months. The four-week average dropped to about 198,000.
beats.means: The job market is cooling through slow hiring, not through layoffs. That gives the Federal Reserve no reason to drop its plan to raise rates in December.
beats.fx: Low layoffs + Fed hike still expected in December → a small support for the dollar and a small weight on gold.

impact.why: Few layoffs keep the case for a December Fed hike intact.
Firmer rate-hike odds make gold, which pays no interest, less appealing.

items.watch: Whether claims stay this low into the next US jobs report.

items.headline: investingLive European session wrap: Dollar, yen and bonds kick it old school
items.story_title: Thursday's flight to safety: shares down, bonds up
items.summary: A classic nervous-market morning in Europe: the franc hit a three-month high against the euro and the yen led the major currencies.

beats.was: Tension between the US and Iran, doubts about AI spending, and France's budget troubles have all been weighing on markets this week.
beats.happened: In European trading, the euro fell to about 0.92 Swiss francs, its lowest in three months, and the dollar slid to about 157 yen. European shares fell and the gap between French and German borrowing costs widened to its largest since 2011.
beats.means: When investors get nervous they buy the franc and the yen; France's troubles add a euro-specific reason to sell.
beats.fx: Shelter buying + French debt worries → franc and yen up, euro down against both.

impact.why: The franc reached a three-month high against the euro on shelter buying.
French debt worries add to the euro's slide.
The yen led the major currencies as shares fell.

items.watch: Whether the Swiss National Bank signals any concern about a strong franc.

items.headline: Oil prices gain on worries of Iran-US escalations after midterms
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: Oil climbed to its highest since May, with Brent above $111 and US crude near $99, on fears that fighting with Iran restarts after the US midterm elections on November 3.

beats.was: The US-Iran war began in late February, and Iran still keeps the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, largely shut. President Trump has been looking for ways to bring fuel prices down before the midterm elections on November 3.
beats.happened: A New York Times report said the US and Israel have plans for new strikes on Iran after the elections, and Saudi Arabia reported attacks on Dammam's airport and an Aramco oil field. Trump said he will not attack Iran before the vote and suggested fuel prices will fall afterwards. Brent rose above $111 a barrel and US crude went past $99.
beats.means: Markets now see the weeks after the vote as the riskier stretch for oil supply, so promises of calm before it do little to cool prices.
beats.fx: Talk of strikes after the election → more risk to Gulf oil → dearer oil. Dearer oil keeps US inflation worries alive, which is why traders fully expect a Federal Reserve hike in December. The lens: whether Brent holds above $110 into November.

impact.why: Fear of renewed strikes on Iran after the election lifted oil to a five-month high.
Higher oil prices lift Canada's export earnings.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a dearer barrel raises its import bill.
Dear oil supports Fed hike bets, but war fear also hits US shares.

items.watch: Brent near $111, and any sign the post-election strike plans move forward or are shelved.

items.headline: French yields cross 5%, spread widest since 2011
items.story_title: France: budget fight, protests and debt worries
items.summary: The extra interest France pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years reached its widest since the euro-zone debt crisis of 2011, a day before Moody's reviews France's credit rating.

beats.was: France's government is trying to pass a 2027 budget that aims to cut the deficit to 5% of national income, but parliament is split and street protests are growing. Investors have been demanding more to lend to France for weeks.
beats.happened: France's 10-year borrowing cost rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, and the gap over Germany widened to roughly 165 basis points, up from about 150 earlier this month. For a short time France paid more than the US to borrow for 10 years, a first since 2013. The vote on the budget's tax side has been delayed, and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said the government could force it through without a vote if needed.
beats.means: Investors now treat France as a real credit worry, not just a political one. More than half of French debt is held abroad, so a downgrade could push foreign money out of the euro area.
beats.fx: Wider France–Germany gap + rating review Friday → money leaves euro-area bonds, which weighs on the euro and tends to help the franc and the pound against it.

impact.why: Rising French borrowing costs pull money out of the euro area.
Euro-area stress sends some money to the franc; the euro hit a three-month low against it.

items.watch: Moody's review of France's credit rating on October 23, and whether the government forces the budget through.

items.headline: US pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia but denies wider Gulf withdrawal
items.story_title: Saudi Arabia: Houthi attacks on oil and airports
items.summary: The US told non-emergency staff and families to leave Saudi Arabia after a deadly Houthi attack on an airport in Dammam, and Brent oil stayed above $110.

beats.was: Yemen's Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran, have stepped up drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia during the US-Iran war, which began in late February. On October 21 a drone aimed at Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oilfield was shot down and two people died.
beats.happened: A late attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in Saudi Arabia's oil-rich east, killed two people and hurt eight; the airport has reopened. The US State Department ordered non-emergency staff and families out of Saudi Arabia and said the order covers only that country, though US officials told Reuters families would also leave other Gulf missions. Brent was above $110 a barrel.
beats.means: Attacks are reaching Saudi Arabia's oil region itself, not just ships at sea, so the risk to the world's biggest oil exporter is rising.
beats.fx: Houthi strikes on Saudi soil → more risk to oil supply → dearer oil and demand for shelter currencies. The lens: whether attacks hit Saudi oil output or export terminals.

impact.why: Attacks near Saudi oil sites raise the risk of lost supply from the biggest exporter.
Rising war risk tends to bring money into the franc.
Higher oil prices lift Canada's export earnings.
Japan pays more for imported oil, but war fear also draws shelter money to the yen.

items.watch: Whether the attacks stop, or whether a strike damages Saudi oil output or a US base.

items.headline: UK factory output expected to stabilise, CBI survey shows
items.story_title: UK: how the economy is holding up
items.summary: British factory orders fell sharply in October, a business survey shows, though firms expect output to stop shrinking and plan to raise prices more.

beats.was: The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), a business lobby, asks manufacturers each month about orders and plans. Official figures show factory output growing this year, and the Bank of England is expected to raise rates on November 5 because inflation is 3.5%.
beats.happened: The CBI's measure of order books dropped to -32 in October from -9 in September, meaning far more firms reported weak orders than strong ones. Firms' outlook for output over the next three months improved to about flat, from deeply negative in July, and their plans to raise prices rose to +24 from +11. The CBI pointed to falling orders and growing staff shortages.
beats.means: Demand for British goods is soft, but factories plan bigger price rises, which is what the Bank of England worries about.
beats.fx: weak orders + firmer price plans → little change to the case for a November hike, a small dent in the growth story for the pound. The lens: the official UK business surveys out on October 23.

impact.why: Weaker orders hurt the growth picture, but higher price plans back the case for rate hikes.

items.watch: Whether official surveys and data confirm falling demand, which could make the Bank of England more cautious after November.

items.headline: Iran Claims Seven Ships Hit in Persian Gulf as Oil Prices Surge
items.story_title: Hormuz: Iran's attacks on Gulf shipping
items.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they hit or mined seven ships in the Gulf in a day, and Brent oil rose above $111 a barrel.

beats.was: Since the US-Iran war began, Iran has kept most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carries about a fifth of the world's oil, blocked or under threat, while US-Iran peace talks have stalled.
beats.happened: The naval arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed it struck four tankers moving oil between ships in the northern Gulf, and that three more vessels hit mines west of Hormuz. These are Iran's own claims and have not been confirmed. It also warned of a wider response against US bases. Yemen's Houthis, who are allied with Iran, kept firing drones at Saudi oilfields, and the US told non-essential staff to leave Saudi Arabia. Brent rose more than 2% in Asian trading.
beats.means: Shipping in the Gulf looks less safe again, not more, so the oil supply risk is growing rather than fading.
beats.fx: Gulf ships under attack → dearer oil → support for oil exporters like Canada, a heavier bill for big oil importers like Japan, and more demand for shelter currencies. The lens: whether these claims are confirmed by shipping trackers.

impact.why: Fresh attacks on tankers in the Gulf add to the risk that less oil gets out.
More war risk tends to bring money into the Swiss franc.
Higher oil prices lift Canada's export earnings.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, which hurts the yen, but war fear also draws shelter money to it.

items.watch: Whether ship trackers and insurers confirm the attacks, and whether the US answers them.

items.headline: SNB Flags Franc Carry-Trade Appeal as FX Intervention Readiness Eases
items.story_title: SNB: the franc and the zero rate
items.summary: Notes from the Swiss National Bank's September meeting say it no longer needs to stand extra ready to sell francs, and that the franc has become a popular currency to borrow in.

beats.was: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) held its rate at 0% in September. Earlier in the year it had said it was more willing than usual to step into currency markets to stop the franc getting too strong.
beats.happened: A summary of the September discussion, published October 22, says the franc fell about 3% against its main partners between June and September, which eased conditions more than slightly higher Swiss rates tightened them. It says wider gaps between interest rates abroad and calm markets have made the franc attractive to borrow cheaply and invest elsewhere, while demand for it as a safe place stayed limited. Inflation was 0.8% in August, mostly from fuel, and growth was solid, so an increased willingness to intervene is no longer needed, though the bank can still act.
beats.means: The SNB is relaxed about the franc for now. It is not trying to push it down, and with near-zero rates the franc tends to be sold when markets are calm.
beats.fx: SNB steps back + franc cheap to borrow → less official selling of francs, but steady pressure from investors who borrow in francs to buy higher-yielding currencies. The lens: whether war fear keeps outweighing that.

impact.why: Less threat of SNB selling helps the franc, but its use as a cheap currency to borrow in weighs on it.

items.watch: Whether the franc jumps on Gulf news and the SNB starts warning again; the next SNB decision is in December.

items.headline: ECB caught in the French drama
items.story_title: European Central Bank: hold now, hike in December?
items.summary: ING's chief eurozone economist, Carsten Brzeski, expects the European Central Bank to hold next week, and says France's debt troubles reduce the need for more hikes.

beats.was: The European Central Bank has raised rates this year as oil pushed inflation up, and markets expected at least one more hike by December. Then France's budget crisis sent its borrowing costs soaring.
beats.happened: Brzeski expects no change next week, with any further hike left to December. He argues higher bond yields are already doing the bank's work: worth about a quarter-point hike for Germany and closer to half a point for France.
beats.means: If markets are already tightening money for the ECB, it has less reason to raise rates itself. A rescue bond-buying tool exists, but France would likely need to pass a budget within EU rules first.
beats.fx: Fewer ECB hikes than the Bank of England → less support for the euro, especially against the pound.

impact.why: A softer ECB path removes some support for the euro; this is one bank's view.

items.watch: The ECB decision next week, and whether its president Christine Lagarde mentions France or its bond-buying backstop.

items.headline: Gold sticks to intraday bearish tone below $4,100 amid Fed hike bets
items.story_title: Gold: rate-hike odds vs war risk
items.summary: Gold slipped below $4,100 an ounce, near its lowest this month, because markets expect a US rate hike in December.

beats.was: Gold had been stuck between about $4,100 and $4,200 for more than two weeks, pulled up by war fears and down by the prospect of higher US rates.
beats.happened: It broke below $4,100 even though the dollar was soft. Futures pricing shows about a 90% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, after hot US inflation data and costly oil. Fed officials have signalled no hurry to act at their October 27–28 meeting.
beats.means: Expected rate hikes are weighing on gold more than war fears are helping it, since gold pays no interest.
beats.fx: Higher expected US rates → holding gold costs more → gold lower. The lens: whether it holds above this month's low.

impact.why: A likely December Fed hike makes interest-paying assets more attractive than gold.

items.watch: Any sign the Fed might wait past December, or a sharp escalation in the Iran war that sends money into gold.

items.headline: Iran's floating oil reserves in Asia run dry under US naval blockade, WSJ reports
items.story_title: US sanctions on Iran's oil shipping
items.summary: Iran's stock of oil stored on tankers off Asia, once close to 90 million barrels, has run out under the US naval blockade.

beats.was: Since the US blockade began, Iran had kept selling to Asian buyers, mostly in China, from oil already parked on ships near Malaysia and Singapore.
beats.happened: Ship trackers cited by the Wall Street Journal say that stored oil fell below 1 million barrels by early October. The US says the blockade has cost Iran at least $25 billion, and Iran's currency has lost about a third of its value since July. Chinese refiners are turning to Brazil and West Africa, while other Gulf exports through Hormuz are back above pre-war levels under US escort.
beats.means: Iran's money squeeze is getting tighter, which raises pressure on it to deal, but also the risk it lashes out at shipping.
beats.fx: Iranian barrels gone → tighter supply for Asian buyers; other Gulf oil flowing again → an offset. The lens: a slow squeeze, not a sudden shock.

impact.why: Iran's lost supply is being partly made up by other Gulf exporters shipping under US protection.

items.watch: Whether Iran answers the squeeze with more attacks on ships or a return to talks.

items.headline: US and Israel plan specific renewed Iran strikes after US midterms, New York Times reports
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: The US and Israeli militaries have reportedly drawn up plans for a short, heavy round of strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3, though President Trump has not signed off.

beats.was: Talks to end the US-Iran war have stalled over Iran's enriched uranium, the US keeps a naval blockade on Iranian oil, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, a key Gulf oil route, largely shut.
beats.happened: The New York Times, citing US officials, said the two militaries have plans to hit Iran's nuclear sites, missiles and drones, and some energy sites, with three US aircraft carriers in place by early November. Trump has turned down similar plans several times this year.
beats.means: The chance of the war flaring again in November just went up, and the threat may be meant to push Iran back to the table. Iranian figures have warned they would hit back at Saudi oil plants and undersea internet cables.
beats.fx: More risk of new strikes → more fear for Gulf oil supply → oil and safe havens like the franc and gold stay supported. The lens: Brent held near $110 in Asia, with no sharp move yet.

impact.why: A planned new round of strikes, with Iranian threats against Saudi oil, keeps a war premium in crude.
Higher odds of renewed war add to demand for the franc as a safe place to park money.
War risk supports gold as a shelter, though rate-hike bets still cap it.

items.watch: Whether Trump approves the plans, and Israel's election on October 27, which could change the timing.

items.headline: Yen set for biggest rally in a month; risk-averse investors shun dollar
items.story_title: Markets turn nervous: AI spending, oil and France
items.summary: The yen had its best day in about a month, with the dollar down to around 157.3 yen, as worries about tech stocks, dear oil and France sent money looking for safety.

beats.was: For most of October the yen sat in a tight range near 158 per dollar, held down by Japan's low interest rates even as Bank of Japan officials hinted at a hike in December.
beats.happened: On Thursday the dollar fell about 0.6% against the yen, its biggest drop since late September, and the yen also gained on the euro, the pound and the Australian dollar. Share markets slid on fears that heavy AI spending won't pay off, Brent oil rose above $111 on Gulf attacks, and France's borrowing costs stayed near their highest since 2002. Falling US government bond yields also took some shine off the dollar. The euro held near $1.123 and the pound near $1.340.
beats.means: When stocks wobble, investors still reach for the yen as a shelter, which can outweigh the damage dear oil does to Japan.
beats.fx: Nervous stock markets → money into shelter → a firmer yen and a softer dollar. The lens: whether the share sell-off deepens or fades.

impact.why: Shelter buying gave the yen its biggest one-day gain in about a month.
Lower US bond yields and fewer bets on extra Fed hikes weighed on the dollar.
The Australian dollar tends to slip when investors get nervous about stocks.

items.watch: Whether stocks steady, and the Bank of Japan meeting on October 29–30.

items.headline: Asian Stocks Sink to 3-mth Low on Tech Angst, Gulf Tensions
items.story_title: Markets turn nervous: AI spending, oil and France
items.summary: Asian shares fell to their lowest in nearly three months as chip stocks sold off and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia raised the risk of a wider Gulf war.

beats.was: Tech and AI companies have carried share markets for much of the year, but investors have grown uneasy about how much these firms are spending and how dear borrowing has become.
beats.happened: A broad index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan fell 1.8%, heading for a fourth weekly loss. Korea's market dropped more than 4%, Hong Kong's more than 3% and Japan's Nikkei about 2%, led by chipmakers such as Tokyo Electron and SK Hynix. Plans by Meta, the Facebook owner, to raise money with a new class of shares revived fears about AI spending. US and European share futures fell too, Brent oil rose above $111, gold eased to about $4,068 and US 10-year bond yields dropped to about 5.09% as money moved to safety.
beats.means: Investors are pulling back from riskier bets just as the Gulf war heats up again, which favours shelter assets over growth-linked currencies.
beats.fx: Falling shares → less appetite for risk → support for the yen and franc, pressure on the Australian and New Zealand dollars. The lens: whether the slide spreads to Wall Street.

impact.why: Weaker Asian shares and chip demand worries hurt the region's most-traded risk currency.
Investors moving to safety tend to buy the yen.
The kiwi usually falls with Asian stocks.
Nervous markets add to demand for the Swiss franc.

items.watch: How Wall Street opens, and whether more Gulf attacks are confirmed.

items.headline: Pound edges higher, outperforming as investor nerves rattle euro zone markets
items.story_title: Pound vs euro: rate gap and France's debt
items.summary: The pound held near $1.34 as money left euro-area markets; the euro is on course for its biggest monthly fall against the pound since May 2023.

beats.was: UK inflation came in above forecast this week, so traders see the Bank of England raising rates on November 5, while France's budget fight has pushed its borrowing costs to the highest in more than 20 years.
beats.happened: Traders now expect at least three quarter-point Bank of England hikes by April, against about two from the European Central Bank. French 10-year yields hit a new 24-year high, Italian and Belgian yields jumped, and European shares fell about 1%. UK bonds held steady. Options traders are the most negative on the euro against the pound since mid-2024.
beats.means: Higher UK rates and France's debt worries both pull money from the euro toward the pound.
beats.fx: Wider UK-euro rate gap + French debt stress → pound up against the euro. The lens: the UK budget on October 28 and France's budget vote on October 27.

impact.why: Money is leaving euro-area bonds and shares as French borrowing costs climb.
More Bank of England hikes are expected than ECB hikes, which favours the pound.

items.watch: Whether UK Chancellor John Healey's October 28 budget calms or rattles bond investors, and whether France passes its budget.

items.headline: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq tumble as oil climbs, investors weigh Meta, Tesla earnings
items.story_title: Thursday's flight to safety: shares down, bonds up
items.summary: US shares fell sharply at Thursday's open, led by tech, while investors piled into US government bonds and pushed their yields down hard.

beats.was: Worries that big tech firms are spending too much on AI had already knocked shares on Wednesday, and Brent oil was climbing on attacks around the Gulf.
beats.happened: The Nasdaq dropped about 2% and the S&P 500 about 1.2% soon after the open. The 10-year US Treasury yield fell about 0.11 percentage point to near 5.02%, as Brent reached a five-month high above $111.
beats.means: Investors are moving from shares into safe bonds, and lower US yields make holding dollars a little less rewarding.
beats.fx: Falling US yields + money leaving shares → pressure on the dollar against the yen and franc; a softer mood also tends to weigh on the Australian dollar.

impact.why: A big one-day drop in US bond yields trims the dollar's rate advantage.
Falling shares send money to the yen as a shelter.
The Aussie usually slips when shares fall.

items.watch: Whether the share sell-off deepens into Friday or buyers return after the big tech earnings.

items.headline: Canadian dollar strengthens as oil prices, BoC rate hike bets support loonie
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: an October 28 rate hike?
items.summary: The Canadian dollar rose for a sixth straight day against the US dollar, helped by higher oil and bets on a Bank of Canada rate hike.

beats.was: Canada is a big oil exporter, so dearer oil tends to help its currency. Traders have come to expect the Bank of Canada to raise its rate on October 28.
beats.happened: The US dollar fell to about 1.4025 Canadian dollars, its lowest since September 21, after drone attacks on Saudi and Russian energy sites lifted oil. Markets see a quarter-point hike to 2.50% as likely.
beats.means: Two supports are working together for the loonie: a higher price for what Canada sells, and a central bank expected to raise rates.
beats.fx: Dearer oil + a likely Bank of Canada hike → steady support for the Canadian dollar.

impact.why: Oil and hike bets keep lifting the loonie, though much is already expected.
The US dollar has lost ground against the loonie six days running.

items.watch: Canada's retail sales figures on Friday, October 23, and the Bank of Canada decision on October 28.

items.headline: Iran tells US to prove it wants peace by lifting blockade
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: Iran's foreign minister said Tehran would give talks another chance, but only if the US first lifts its naval blockade on Iranian oil.

beats.was: Efforts to end the US-Iran war are stuck, and the US Navy has been stopping Iran from selling oil by sea.
beats.happened: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the US must lift the blockade to show it is serious, and warned a new war would end badly for Washington. An unnamed Iranian official threatened US political figures if strikes resume, and US officials said some American troops are quietly being pulled back from Middle East bases.
beats.means: The door to talks is open a crack, but on terms the US has so far rejected, so no quick deal is likely.
beats.fx: Talk of diplomacy → a little less war risk → oil could ease; tough conditions and threats → the war premium stays. The lens: US crude was little changed near $97.60.

impact.why: An offer to talk is offset by conditions the US is unlikely to accept and new threats.

items.watch: Any US reply on the blockade, or a date for new talks.

items.headline: New Zealand's CPI inflation eases to 3.7% YoY in Q3, vs 3.8% expected
items.story_title: RBNZ: the October 28 decision
items.summary: New Zealand's inflation slowed to 3.7% in the third quarter, a little below forecasts, which takes some heat out of the bet on a rate hike next week.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand had forecast inflation of 3.9% and markets gave roughly 80% odds that it raises rates on October 28. The kiwi had climbed for five days on that bet.
beats.happened: Prices rose 0.7% over the quarter and 3.7% from a year earlier, down from 4.1% and below the 3.8% expected. Cheaper petrol and diesel did most of the pulling down; prices of local services barely slowed.
beats.means: A small miss, not a change of story: inflation is still well above the bank's 1–3% target, so a hike stays likely, but the case is less urgent and later hikes look less certain.
beats.fx: Softer inflation → slightly lower odds of RBNZ hikes → kiwi eases. The lens: it slipped back just under 57 US cents, giving up only a small part of its recent climb.

impact.why: Inflation came in under both forecasts and the central bank's own projection, trimming hike bets.

items.watch: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's decision on October 28.

items.headline: Gold rebounds above $4,130 as Oil retreats, Fed decision looms
items.story_title: Gold: oil, yields and the Fed
items.summary: Gold bounced back to about $4,133 after three days of losses, as oil slipped and the dollar eased, but it's still stuck in the same narrow range.

beats.was: Gold is down about a quarter from its record near $5,600 because costly oil has pushed the US Federal Reserve toward raising interest rates, which makes gold, paying no interest, less attractive. It has traded between $4,100 and $4,200 for 16 days in a row.
beats.happened: Gold rose to about $4,133 after touching $4,106 earlier on Wednesday, helped by a dip in oil after a US sanctions licence and a slightly weaker dollar. Markets still see about an 89% chance the Fed raises rates in December, and a small chance at its October 27–28 meeting.
beats.means: The bounce is small and doesn't change the bigger picture: as long as a Fed rate hike is expected, gold struggles to climb. Cheaper oil would ease that pressure.
beats.fx: Oil dips → slightly less pressure for Fed hikes → gold lifts a little. The lens: still inside its range; the Fed meeting next week matters more.

impact.why: A small rebound as oil and the dollar eased.
The dollar slipped slightly as oil fell.

items.watch: The Fed's October 27–28 decision and next week's US core inflation (PCE) figure.

items.headline: Risk-on trade as desks cite OFAC authorising offloading of some cargo involving some blocked vessels
items.story_title: US sanctions on Iran's oil shipping
items.summary: The US Treasury let some cargo be unloaded from tankers it had just blacklisted, and oil slipped while shares, bonds and gold rose.

beats.was: The US is at war with Iran and blocks Iranian oil exports, adding tankers and shipping firms to its sanctions list most weeks. Oil had climbed back near five-month highs on Wednesday morning as peace talks stalled.
beats.happened: The US Treasury's sanctions office (OFAC) blacklisted nine more vessels and several shipping firms on Wednesday, but issued a licence allowing some of their cargo to be unloaded and their business wound down. US crude fell about 80 cents soon after, and the dollar eased.
beats.means: Oil already at sea may still reach buyers instead of being stuck, so a little less supply goes missing. The licence is narrow, and past ones like it have had little lasting effect.
beats.fx: Some blocked oil can still be delivered → slightly more supply → small dip in oil prices → mild relief for oil importers like Japan and Europe, a small drag on the Canadian dollar. The lens: a narrow, technical step, not a change in US policy.

impact.why: Lets some sanctioned cargo reach buyers, easing supply worries a little.
Gold rose as bond yields and the dollar eased on the move.
The dollar slipped as cheaper oil eased Fed rate-hike worries.

items.watch: Whether the US widens the licence, or new sanctions follow that block more Iranian oil.

items.headline: US treasury sells $13 billion of 20 year bonds at a high yield of 5.469%
items.story_title: US government borrowing: who's buying the bonds
items.summary: The US government sold $13 billion of 20-year bonds at about 5.47%, slightly above where they traded just before, with foreign buyers taking a smaller share than usual.

beats.was: The US Treasury sells long-term bonds at regular auctions to fund the government. How eagerly investors buy shows how much they are willing to lend at current rates; weak demand pushes borrowing costs up.
beats.happened: Wednesday's sale cleared at 5.469%, a little above the pre-sale level and above last month's 5.42%. Overall demand was above average, but the share taken by foreign and other outside investors was well below normal, with US buyers filling the gap.
beats.means: A middling result: the government had no trouble borrowing, but softer interest from overseas buyers is a quiet warning sign for long-term US borrowing costs. Yields barely moved afterwards.
beats.fx: Mixed demand → no clear move in US yields → little effect on the dollar. The lens: watch whether foreign demand stays soft at the next long-bond sales.

impact.why: Adequate demand overall but a smaller foreign share; yields barely reacted.

items.watch: Next week's 2-, 5- and 7-year US Treasury note sales and the Fed's October 27–28 meeting.

items.headline: US crude stocks fall 3.06 million barrels, more than the 0.82 million expected
items.story_title: US oil stocks: a run of draws
items.summary: Official US figures showed crude and gasoline stocks both fell more than expected last week, the second big weekly drop in a row.

beats.was: Oil has been near five-month highs because attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea threaten Gulf supply. The week before, US crude stocks fell about 8.6 million barrels, and an industry estimate on Tuesday had pointed to another large drop.
beats.happened: The US Energy Information Administration said crude stocks fell about 3.1 million barrels in the week to October 16, against about 0.8 million expected. Gasoline stocks fell about 3 million barrels, while diesel and heating oil stocks rose.
beats.means: America is drawing down its own stored oil while Gulf supply is at risk, so there is less cushion if shipping gets worse. The drop was smaller than Tuesday's industry estimate, so US crude barely moved, near $98.
beats.fx: Shrinking US oil stocks → less spare supply → keeps oil prices firm → helps the Canadian dollar, weighs on big oil importers like Japan. The lens: mostly expected after Tuesday's estimate, so the push is small.

impact.why: A second large weekly fall in US stocks adds to supply worries, though much was already expected.
Firm oil prices support Canada's export income.

items.watch: Next week's US stock figures and any news on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

items.headline: France's 10-year bond yield climbs above 5%, stirring fears of a credit crisis
items.story_title: France: budget fight, protests and debt worries
items.summary: France now pays over 5% to borrow for ten years, the first time since 2002, and the gap over German debt is the widest since the euro debt crisis of 2009–2011.

beats.was: France's government has no majority to pass spending cuts, its debt is about 119% of the economy, and student protests have turned violent, with partial curfews in some cities. The budget vote is due October 27.
beats.happened: The 10-year French government bond yield went above 5%. The extra yield over Germany's 10-year bond widened to roughly 1.6 percentage points, a level last seen in the 2009–2011 crisis.
beats.means: Investors are asking more to lend to France because they doubt it can control its debt before next year's election. That worry spills into the euro as a whole.
beats.fx: French borrowing costs up + wider gap to Germany → doubts about the euro area's weakest big borrower → money leaves the euro for safer homes like the franc. The lens: a budget deal or calmer protests would ease it.

impact.why: Higher French borrowing costs feed doubts about the euro area and cap the euro's recovery.
Stress inside the euro area sends money to the Swiss franc next door.

items.watch: The October 27 budget vote, this weekend's protests, and Moody's review of France's credit rating on Friday.

items.headline: BOJ likely to raise rates every three months, former official says
items.story_title: BoJ: the road to the next hike
items.summary: Eiji Maeda, a former Bank of Japan executive who ran its policy work, expects the bank to keep raising rates about once every three months, starting in December.

beats.was: The Bank of Japan has been lifting its rates slowly from near zero. It is expected to hold at its October 29–30 meeting, with most bets on a hike in December.
beats.happened: In a Bloomberg interview, Maeda said he expects the next hike in December and another in March or April, calling a roughly three-month pace appropriate to keep inflation near target. Markets price about an 80% chance of a hike by December.
beats.means: A steady path of hikes would slowly narrow the gap between Japanese and US rates, which is what has kept the yen weak. It is a former official's view, not a bank decision.
beats.fx: Firmer expectations of regular BoJ hikes → a little support for the yen. The lens: the yen is still weak near 158 per dollar because oil keeps Japan's import bill high.

impact.why: Adds weight to a December hike and more after it, though it is an outside view.

items.watch: The Bank of Japan's October 29–30 meeting and its updated inflation forecasts.

items.headline: Australian Dollar extends recovery as hawkish RBA offsets USD strength
items.story_title: RBA: the November 3 decision
items.summary: The Australian dollar reached a one-month high near 70.3 US cents, a fourth day of gains, as Reserve Bank of Australia officials kept the door open to a November hike.

beats.was: The Aussie fell below 69 US cents last week, its lowest since early July, before Reserve Bank of Australia officials turned more worried about inflation.
beats.happened: Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser warned that underlying inflation for July-September may come in hotter than forecast, and Assistant Governor Christopher Kent said the 'neutral' rate, neither boosting nor slowing the economy, seems to be rising.
beats.means: Both point the same way: rates may need to go higher. Better-than-expected growth in China, Australia's biggest customer, also helps.
beats.fx: Hike talk → higher Australian rates ahead → support for the Aussie. A firmer US dollar on Fed hike bets is the brake.

impact.why: Officials' hawkish comments keep a November hike alive.

items.watch: Australia's July-September inflation figures, due late October, the last big input before the November 3 decision.

items.headline: UK inflation jumps more than expected fuelling rate hike expectations
items.story_title: UK: inflation, borrowing and the Oct 28 budget
items.summary: Alongside hotter inflation, UK government borrowing for September came in above forecast, a week before Chancellor Rachel Reeves' budget on October 28.

beats.was: UK government bond yields hit a 19-year high in September on worries about how much the government borrows, and the budget lands October 28.
beats.happened: The government borrowed £24.5bn in September, more than expected. Borrowing so far this tax year is about £6bn above the official forecast, and total debt passed £3 trillion for the first time.
beats.means: Higher borrowing leaves less room in the budget and keeps debt worries alive, at the same time as inflation pushes the Bank of England toward a hike.
beats.fx: Rate hikes help the pound, but debt worries hurt it. Together they cancelled out on Wednesday morning: the pound barely moved.

impact.why: Debt worries offset the lift from a likely rate hike.

items.watch: The October 28 budget: tax rises or spending cuts that calm bond markets would help the pound.

items.headline: Japanese Yen ticks up within previous range, buoyed by hawkish BoJ comments
items.story_title: BoJ: the road to the next hike
items.summary: Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino said Japan's underlying inflation is close to the 2% goal, leaving room for more rate hikes; the yen edged up but stayed near 158 per dollar.

beats.was: The yen has been weak for weeks, near 158 per dollar, partly because Japan's rates are far below US rates. Markets expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates again, most likely on December 17.
beats.happened: Himino said underlying inflation is near target, borrowing conditions are still easy, and longer-run inflation expectations are rising.
beats.means: A deputy governor saying inflation is near target is a hint that the bank is getting ready to raise rates again.
beats.fx: More signals of a hike → smaller gap with US rates over time → slow support for the yen. A wider-than-expected trade deficit in September limited the lift.

impact.why: Supports the case for a December Bank of Japan hike, which is already expected.

items.watch: The Bank of Japan meeting next week, and whether it raises its inflation forecasts.

items.headline: United Kingdom CPI inflation climbs to 3.5% YoY in September, vs. 3.4% expected
items.story_title: BoE: the November decision
items.summary: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, a touch above the 3.4% forecast and the highest in a year, as fuel costs from the US-Iran war fed into prices.

beats.was: The Bank of England, whose rate is 3.75% against a 2% inflation target, has not raised rates since 2023, but a strong jobs report had markets nearly sure of a quarter-point hike at its November 5 meeting.
beats.happened: Prices rose 3.5% over the year to September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% expected. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, about as forecast.
beats.means: Inflation is running well above the 2% goal and moving the wrong way, mostly from petrol and diesel. That makes a November hike very hard for the Bank to skip.
beats.fx: Higher inflation → November hike all but locked in → UK rates stay attractive → support for the pound. Most of this was already expected, so the lift is modest.

impact.why: A higher-than-expected figure backs a November Bank of England hike.

items.watch: Whether the Bank signals more than one hike; a quick fall in oil would ease the pressure.

items.headline: Euro weakens below 1.1250 as French protests and fiscal risks weigh
items.story_title: France: unrest, budget vote and the euro
items.summary: The euro slipped to about $1.1225 as France prepared to use some military forces to keep order during new protests expected this weekend.

beats.was: France has seen widespread protests over its budget, and investors already ask about 1.5 percentage points more to lend to France for ten years than to Germany, a sign of worry about its debts.
beats.happened: Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said curfews would be used where needed, and officials plan to bring in some troops for this weekend's protests. The euro fell back below $1.125 in Asian trading. ECB President Christine Lagarde and other ECB officials speak later Wednesday.
beats.means: Unrest in the eurozone's second-largest economy keeps a lid on the euro even when oil eases.
beats.fx: More unrest in France → more worry about French debt → investors demand more to hold it → weaker euro. The lens: calm protests and a passed budget would ease this.

impact.why: French unrest and debt worries weigh on the single currency.
Europe's worries send some money to the franc next door.

items.watch: This weekend's French protests, ECB speeches Wednesday, and France's budget vote on October 27.

items.headline: Japan's Katayama sees no gap with BOJ, says wage-driven inflation is near
items.story_title: BoJ: when the next hike comes
items.summary: Japan's Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told parliament the government and the Bank of Japan see things the same way, and that pay-driven inflation is close, a condition the BoJ wants before raising rates again.

beats.was: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government plans a consumption tax cut and cash handouts, and investors have worried it could clash with the Bank of Japan's rate rises; in September two board members picked by the government voted against the hike to 1.25%.
beats.happened: Katayama said today's price rises come mostly from import costs, but the economy is close to inflation driven by rising wages. Asked about a clash with the BoJ, she said the two sides talk and she sees no gap. She did not openly back more hikes.
beats.means: It lowers the odds that the government stands in the way of the next hike, which most economists expect in December.
beats.fx: Less political pushback → a December BoJ hike looks safer → mild support for the yen. The lens: do the government's picks on the board keep dissenting?

impact.why: Eases fears that the government blocks further rate rises.

items.watch: Friday's Japan inflation figures and the BoJ's Oct 29–30 meeting, including how its board votes.

items.headline: Oil rises on Middle East supply and shipping concerns
items.story_title: Hormuz: mines, tanker hits and blockade threats
items.summary: Brent crude climbed back toward $110 in Asian trading after Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a supertanker caught fire on a mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, and analysts said ship attacks now reach the Gulf of Oman.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, has been shut since the US-Iran war began this month, and Gulf exporters have leaned on loading points outside it, such as the Gulf of Oman, to keep crude moving.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said a supertanker hit a sea mine and caught fire south of the strait. LSEG analysts said attacks have spread as far as the Gulf of Oman; the ship tracker Kpler counts at least 18 attacks on vessels in two weeks. Yemen's Houthi rebels also claimed strikes on Saudi oil sites at Yanbu and Shaybah. Brent rose about 0.8% to $109.64.
beats.means: The workaround routes that kept Middle East oil flowing are now in range too, so a quick return to normal supply looks less likely even while mediation talks go on.
beats.fx: Attacks outside the strait → less oil getting out → higher crude → support for oil exporters like Canada, and a bigger import bill for Japan and Europe. The lens: do loadings in the Gulf of Oman actually slow?

impact.why: Attacks are reaching the routes used to bypass the shut strait.
Higher crude lifts Canada's export income.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a costlier barrel weighs on the yen.

items.watch: Whether tanker loadings off Oman drop, and any reply to Iran's mediation offer; Wednesday's US crude stock report.

items.headline: Japan exports rise 16.7% for 13th straight month on AI chip demand, trade gap narrows
items.story_title: Japan: exports, the oil bill and the yen
items.summary: Japan's exports grew 16.7% from a year earlier in September, a 13th straight rise but well short of the 20% expected, so the trade deficit came in wider than forecast at about ¥537 billion.

beats.was: Japan's exports have been lifted all year by demand for chips and AI equipment, while costly oil, pushed up by the Gulf war, has swollen the import bill and kept the country in trade deficit.
beats.happened: Japan's Ministry of Finance said September exports rose 16.7% from a year earlier, against about 20% expected and 19.3% in August. Imports rose 18.9%, slower than August's 28%. The deficit was about ¥537 billion, against ¥181 billion expected but half of August's roughly ¥1.1 trillion.
beats.means: Overseas demand for Japanese goods is still solid but cooling, and the energy bill remains the drag. A smaller gap than August helps a little, but the miss gives the Bank of Japan, which meets Oct 29–30, no new reason to hurry a rate rise.
beats.fx: Exports slower than hoped, oil still costly → more yen sold to pay for imports than expected → mild pressure on the yen. The lens: is the oil bill shrinking, or just pausing?

impact.why: Exports missed and the deficit beat forecasts, though it halved from August.

items.watch: The Bank of Japan's Oct 29–30 meeting and its new forecasts; a lasting drop in oil would shrink the import bill.

items.headline: U.S. ordering some government staff to depart Saudi Arabia, reducing military footprint in Middle East
items.story_title: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia
items.summary: The US told non-essential embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia because of Houthi attacks, and US officials say the military is quietly thinning its presence at bases in the region.

beats.was: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group has been firing drones and missiles at Saudi airports and oil sites this month; a strike on Riyadh's main airport killed 12 people. Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil exporter, and with the Strait of Hormuz shut its Red Sea routes matter even more.
beats.happened: The State Department ordered non-essential staff and families out of Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on airports and key infrastructure. Its spokesman said the order covers Saudi Arabia only; other Gulf embassies are on reduced operations. Officials said US forces are cutting their footprint at Middle East posts over Houthi and Iranian threats, and President Trump did not rule out strikes on the Houthis.
beats.means: Washington is treating the threat to Saudi Arabia as serious and lasting, not a passing flare-up. That raises the odds of more attacks on Saudi oil, or of US strikes on the Houthis.
beats.fx: US pulls staff from Saudi Arabia → higher risk to Gulf oil supply on top of Hormuz → keeps a war premium in oil and some demand for the franc. The lens: confirmed hits on Saudi exports would push oil higher; a lull in attacks would let it ease.

impact.why: An evacuation order signals Washington expects the attacks on the top oil exporter to go on.
A wider Gulf conflict keeps some money looking for safety.
The dollar firmed a little on the news as a safe place to park money, but dearer oil also feeds US inflation worries.

items.watch: Any Houthi hit on Saudi oil exports, and whether President Trump orders strikes on the Houthis.

items.headline: Benjamin Netanyahu says IDF, Mossad ordered to overthrow Iranian regime over nukes
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he has told Israel's army and spy agency to work to bring down Iran's government, saying Iran is again trying to build a nuclear bomb.

beats.was: After this year's war, Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, largely shut while indirect US-Iran talks stall. Reports say a renewed US-Israeli bombing campaign was shelved before the US midterm elections.
beats.happened: Speaking at an army officers' graduation on Wednesday, Netanyahu said his instruction to the military and the Mossad is to overthrow Iran's government. Defence Minister Israel Katz warned that Iran would 'burn' if it attacks Israel.
beats.means: It raises the risk that fighting restarts and makes a deal to reopen Hormuz harder. It is a statement of intent during an Israeli election campaign, not an announced operation, and oil barely moved.
beats.fx: Higher risk of renewed war → oil supply worries stay → support for oil and the franc. The lens: markets treat it as rhetoric unless strikes follow.

impact.why: Adds to the risk of renewed conflict around Hormuz; no immediate supply change.
Rising war risk tends to lift demand for the franc as a safe place.

items.watch: Any sign of renewed US or Israeli strikes on Iran, and Iran's response on Hormuz.

items.headline: Iran Intensifies Strikes on Ships
items.story_title: Hormuz: reopening offer vs ship attacks
items.summary: Attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz are getting more frequent and more damaging, with missiles replacing drones and two vessels sunk last week.

beats.was: About a fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the US-Iran war began. Iran has been attacking ships there to pressure Washington while peace talks run through Pakistan and Qatar.
beats.happened: At least 23 attacks on ships were logged in or near the strait in the first two weeks of October, at least five of them hitting engine rooms, which hadn't happened in September. Iran is using more missiles, and at least two ships sank last week.
beats.means: Oil is still flowing: Gulf exports are close to pre-war levels by some counts. But each attack makes tankers scarcer and shipping and insurance dearer, which keeps a risk premium in oil.
beats.fx: Heavier ship attacks → costlier, riskier Gulf shipping → keeps oil prices firm → helps the Canadian dollar, weighs on importers like Japan, and supports safe havens like the Swiss franc. The lens: escalation in kind, but flows are holding up.

impact.why: Worse ship attacks raise shipping costs and the risk of lost supply.
More violence at sea keeps demand for safe havens.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so costlier shipping hurts its trade balance.

items.watch: Any sign that Gulf oil exports fall back below normal, or that attacks ease if talks make progress.

items.headline: US sends more warships as Iran peace push stalls over enriched uranium
items.story_title: US–Iran: a mediated plan to restart talks
items.summary: Iran's top security official told Pakistan's army chief that none of Iran's enriched uranium will leave the country, while the US sent another carrier group and some 9,000 sailors and Marines to the region.

beats.was: The US and Iran have been at war since earlier this year and the Strait of Hormuz, the main Gulf oil route, is shut. Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, has been carrying a plan to restart talks.
beats.happened: Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said no enriched uranium will be sent abroad, a key US demand. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran won't talk under threat. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group and an amphibious group are heading in, and President Trump is said to be weighing new strikes. Gulf stock markets fell.
beats.means: The two sides are stuck on the same nuclear point, and the US is adding force rather than easing off, so a quick reopening of Hormuz looks less likely.
beats.fx: Stalled talks + more warships → Hormuz stays shut longer → oil supply stays tight → firmer oil, steadier demand for safe havens like the franc. The lens: any sign Iran would ship uranium out would reverse this.

impact.why: A stalled peace push and a bigger US fleet point to the oil route staying closed.
Rising war risk keeps money looking for safety.
Canada exports oil, so dearer crude helps its trade income.

items.watch: Whether Trump orders new strikes, and any change in Iran's line on shipping uranium abroad.

items.headline: Middle East War: Iran rejects US terms as tanker explodes near Hormuz
items.story_title: US-Iran: talks on reopening Hormuz
items.summary: Iran turned down US-backed Pakistani talks proposals and said its enriched uranium will not leave the country, while the US is reported to be sending a third aircraft carrier to the region.

beats.was: The Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil, has been shut for months by the US-Iran war, and Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir is in Tehran trying to restart talks.
beats.happened: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said there are no talks until the US meets seven Iranian conditions. Parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Iran had nothing new to say. Fox News reported a third US carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is heading to the region.
beats.means: Tuesday's hopes for a deal have faded, and both sides are hardening. A reopening of the strait looks further away.
beats.fx: Less hope of a deal → oil stays high → support for oil-exporter Canada's dollar, pressure on oil-importer Japan's yen, and demand for shelter like the Swiss franc.

impact.why: Iran's refusal pushes a reopening of Hormuz further off.
More conflict risk adds demand for a safe place to park money.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a higher oil bill weighs on the yen.
Higher oil helps Canada, a big oil exporter.

items.watch: Any US decision on new strikes, or a fresh offer from Pakistan or Qatar that Iran accepts.

items.headline: Australian central banker says policy working, but inflation outlook worse
items.story_title: RBA: the November 3 decision
items.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia's deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, said inflation now looks set to run above the bank's own forecast, raising the odds of another rate rise on November 3. The Aussie pushed above 70 US cents.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia has already raised its cash rate four times this year, to 4.60%, to fight inflation lifted partly by the Gulf war's hit to oil. It next decides on November 3.
beats.happened: Speaking at a Citi conference in Sydney, Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said higher rates are slowing the economy, but the inflation outlook has got clearly worse, partly because of high oil prices. Markets raised the chance of a November hike to 4.85% to about 40%, from 30% at the start of the week, and AUD/USD rose to about 0.701, a two-week high.
beats.means: A senior official saying inflation will beat the bank's forecast keeps a fifth hike on the table, even with unemployment at a five-year high of 4.7% and house prices falling. Next week's third-quarter inflation figure, seen near 4%, is the deciding number.
beats.fx: Inflation running hotter than the RBA expected → more chance of a rate rise → higher returns on Australian dollars → Aussie up. The lens: does next week's inflation figure back him up?

impact.why: Hike odds for Nov 3 rose to about 40% and the Aussie broke above 0.70.

items.watch: Australia's third-quarter inflation figure next week; a soft print, or weaker jobs and housing, would cool hike bets.

items.headline: Bank of England's Greene says inflation risks are bigger than thought
items.story_title: Bank of England: a November 5 hike
items.summary: Megan Greene, a Bank of England rate-setter, said the energy shock could spread into wider inflation more than the bank expected, and backed raising rates.

beats.was: The Bank of England is widely expected to raise rates on November 5, after the war with Iran sent energy prices higher.
beats.happened: In a speech at the London School of Economics, Greene said pay is rising faster than official figures show, the economy has held up well, and current rates may not be holding it back much. She wants to act now and adjust later if needed.
beats.means: A rate-setter arguing for firmness backs the market's view that several UK hikes are coming.
beats.fx: Firm Bank of England voices + hikes already expected → mild, steady support for the pound.

impact.why: Supports the hikes markets already expect rather than adding new ones.

items.watch: The Bank of England decision on November 5 and how many rate-setters vote to hike.
